citation.author: McEvoy, Amalia
citation.title: Digitizing the American West: Analyzing Rhetoric in Red Dead Redemption 2
citation.venue: Seton Hall University MA thesis (Department of English; adviser Dr. Mary Balkun), South Orange, NJ; eRepository ETD #3098

thesis: The long-form narrative game can be 'read' like literature; via reader-response theory (Rosenblatt, Fish) supplemented by Bogost's procedural rhetoric, RDR2's coded systems (above all the Honor system) constitute a rhetoric that persuades players toward moral choice while teaching a compressed slice of American history (1899-1900), even as the game's realism blurs teaching history with romanticizing it.
sections: Opening / framing: long-form games as texts; reader response as lens; The Last of Us as precedent for games delivering social critique
Game Summary: Van der Linde gang arc from the Grizzlies to Arthur's death
Worldbuilding: realism and the 'fourth dimension'; developer interviews; contrast with GTA V
Critical Context: Bogost's procedural rhetoric; Denning's deep play; Bourgonjon's game literacy; Rosenblatt's invisible reader; Fish's interpretive communities
'Playing' History: enemy reduction; work-vs-play; Gilded-Age economic stand-ins
Immigrant Discrimination: Dinnerstein & Reimers; Menchaca and the 1896 Rodriguez case; 'greaser' and Javier
A Return to Rhetoric: realism as carrier of rhetorical/educational merit; completionist player; Ostenson on games in the classroom; the Honor system and the two deaths
concepts: procedural rhetoric (Bogost; secondary, operationally central framework)
play as 'free space of movement within a more rigid structure' (Salen & Zimmerman via Bogost)
edutainment and the gamification of the past
the frontier myth / death of the Wild West
the Other (Native American, Mexican, African American, immigrant representation)
the completionist vs. experiential player ('poetry-seeing eyes' transposed to gamers)
Honor system as the seat of the game's rhetoric
Western genre / closure of the frontier (implicit; Manifest Destiny not named explicitly)
readings: The Honor system is the seat of RDR2's rhetoric: reward/punishment morality meter steers player conduct ('goodness rewarded with peace, misdeeds punished with suffering')
Arthur's two honor-contingent deaths (peaceful sunrise vs. Micah's bullet in the rain) deliver 'the death the player deserves' and dramatize the gap between character-Arthur and avatar-Arthur
In-game consequences for discriminatory player dialogue let Rockstar comment on period bigotry and 'stifle' its expansion today
RDR2 contra GTA V: shared NPC autonomy, but RDR2 forces players to watch society react, raising moral stakes that GTA's consequence-free mayhem dissolves
Economic Othering: Cornwall and the Pinkertons as Vanderbilt/Rockefeller stand-ins; poor gang framed as 'good,' wealthy enemies as 'evil'
Reader-response as the player's better mode: gather meaning from the experience of play rather than 'completing' the game as a task to overcome

game_elements.element: Valentine saloon brawl with Tommy (opening tutorial fight)
game_elements.how_treated: Read for 'dual purpose': combat tutorial plus establishing Arthur's potential dishonor; player may release grip (Tommy lives) or beat him to 'rag-dolling' with an honor penalty and later-visible cranial damage
game_elements.locus: Game Summary / 'Playing' History sections; early game, Valentine

game_elements.element: Honor system (morality meter; coyote negative / buck positive)
game_elements.how_treated: Central case for procedural rhetoric: binary reward/punishment structure that fences players toward moral conduct and governs the endings; identified as 'where the rhetoric of the game lies'
game_elements.locus: Critical Context and A Return to Rhetoric sections; game-wide

game_elements.how_treated: Honor-contingent: peaceful sunrise vs. Micah's gunshot; read as the game delivering a deserved death and the rhetorical payoff of the Honor system
game_elements.locus: A Return to Rhetoric; Beaver Hollow / final act

game_elements.how_treated: Worked example of work-vs-play mastery (Denning); slows time for precise aim but can also kill an innocent horse, costing honor
Flagged as the segment where the player no longer controls Arthur; noted rather than analyzed at length

game_elements.element: Charlotte Braithwaite suffragette mission + recurring Saint Denis suffragette
game_elements.how_treated: Scripted chaperoning of suffragettes to town hall shows Arthur written as respectful; recurring Saint Denis protester is harassed by default NPCs regardless of player conduct, read as Rockstar's realism representing overlooked communities
game_elements.locus: 'Playing' History section; Rhodes and Saint Denis

game_elements.element: Rhodes feud: the Grays (abolitionist) vs. the Braithwaites (plantation owners)
game_elements.how_treated: Region representing Southern states; gang pits families against each other; kidnapping of Jack Marston; read as historical-South setting

game_elements.element: Saint Denis (Angelo Bronte; bank robbery; Hosea executed)
game_elements.how_treated: New Orleans/Louisiana analogue; high-society ball and the fatal bank heist; Bronte fed to alligators; marks Dutch's turn to violence
Oil tycoon and private police force read as Gilded-Age robber-baron stand-ins (Vanderbilts/Rockefellers); the train heist; economic Othering
game_elements.locus: Game Summary and 'Playing' History; train heist, recurring pursuit

game_elements.how_treated: Dying coal town whose tense, sad residents figure industrial decline and the close of the frontier economy

game_elements.element: Mandatory shootouts vs. nameless enemies (e.g., the Pinkertons)
game_elements.how_treated: Instance of 'enemy reduction' (Denning) - aggression leaves no time to weigh humanity; contrasted with preserved humanity of passive NPCs

game_elements.element: Discrimination content: 'darkie' slur (prologue) and 'greaser' (toward Javier, used by NPCs and Bill)
game_elements.how_treated: Read as period-situating language that recalls White-maintained social hierarchies; tied to Menchaca/Dinnerstein immigration history
game_elements.locus: Worldbuilding and Immigrant Discrimination sections; prologue and Javier scenes

game_elements.how_treated: Gaelic/Irish-heritage burial custom (sourced to YouTuber RealPixels) read as a diversity cue among the gang given period nativism

themes: realism as the medium of persuasion
morality and consequence as the game's argument
class collapse at the close of the frontier
player freedom as ethical opportunity and risk
continuity between literary and ludic experience

debate_axis_positions: Education vs. entertainment: both/and - primarily entertainment yet carrying genuine educational/rhetorical merit; concedes developers chase revenue not historians' questions
Realism: pedagogy vs. romanticization - holds the tension open; for some audiences the game's history may be the only history they meet
Narrative vs. systems as locus of meaning: shifts rhetoric away from plot/dialogue toward procedure (Honor system, reactive NPC code), aligning with Bogost against purely narratological readings
Player freedom vs. moral steering: open-world freedom bounded by a moral 'fence' of law, NPC reaction, and honor
tensions: Framework hybridity: reception-side reader-response and production-side procedural rhetoric joined via 'meaning from experience' but the seam is under-theorized
Honor binarism: high/low honor and a 'deserved death' moral economy may flatten gradations and player effort decoupling character from avatar
Persuasion-efficacy claim ('stifles the expansion of those ideologies') asserted without player-reception evidence
Methodological status: single-player close reading plus developer-interview and historical sources; no empirical reception study despite a reader-response frame inviting one
